title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
description: That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course,
body: That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course, given that President Reagan provided material support to Margaret Thatcher during the Falklands War in 1982  – an act which reinforced the long-standing alliance between London and Washington in times of conflict.For Trump, however, that mutual support – the "Special Relationship" – was eroded by Sir Keir Starmer when the UK Government chose not to join the US war on Iran."You weren't there to help me", the president retorted in an interview with GB News this week. The Falklands were "a long way away", he said. The Falkland Islanders – who voted almost unanimously to remain a British overseas territory in 2013 – would point out that distance from London to the Falklands is fractionally shorter than the distance between Washington DC and the US territory of Guam, in the western Pacific.Still, Trump's words have undoubtedly galvanised Milei. As have the opinion polls. He urgently needs a boost ahead of a presidential election next year in which one of his challengers, his estranged vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, has presented herself as a tougher defender of national sovereignty and attacked Milei's diplomatic approach on the Falklands as failing.Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.With two energy companies – the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK – due to undertake work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have.In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally. The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".

schema.headline: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder

title: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
description: "It makes us look a bit like a pirate ship," a senior Reform figure acknowledges privately, deeply frustrated that after a year in which they say the
body: "It makes us look a bit like a pirate ship," a senior Reform figure acknowledges privately, deeply frustrated that after a year in which they say the party has "radically professionalised" the events of the last few days could still happen.It was the recurring conversation throughout Reform UK's conference in Birmingham: the consequences of the undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4 News which has cost two senior party figures their jobs, at least for now.How much damage does it cause to Reform? And what does it tell us about them?"A key part of the appeal of us is the sense of us being cavaliers. Doing things differently. Standing out. And that's great. We have roundheads too. Those who ask the boring questions. Do the checks. We need more of them," this same senior figure adds.The story of Reform over the last 12 months can be summarised in three words: defections, elections and money.Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year – not least the recruitment of former Conservative cabinet ministers Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman.Elections have been as well - Reform's gains in the English local elections and the devolved parliament elections in Wales and in Scotland.But so too has money. The backdrop to this conference was the swirl of questions about money even before Channel 4 News', and Verbatim Investigations', endeavours.In the hour or two before its broadcast on Thursday night, senior Reform figures, including those directly caught up in it, projected a sense of being relatively relaxed about it. Awkward, embarrassing, but survivable.Once it was broadcast, things changed. There was fury, I am told, and very quickly there was a sense of its gravity. "A few bottles of red were had, and we knew we had to act," is how one source described it to me. The conversations went on into the early hours.Firstly, there was anger that it would drown out a conference that has been months in the planning. And yes, it has dominated conversation here in Birmingham.Secondly, there was widespread concern about the image it projected, the impression it would leave.Reform wants to project itself as ready to run the country.Some saw James Orr's work as head of policy as key to that professionalisation. Orr as well as Dan Jukes, a close aide to Nigel Farage, have been suspended and both deny wrongdoing."We need people to see the reality that Reform is getting ready for government," I am told.And yet the headlines allow critics to claim they are not just ramshackle and amateurish but can point to what looks like a pattern of activity, consciously pursued, to breach the law.Absolutely not, Nigel Farage insisted to me, there was no such pattern.But what of the ethos of the party? Journalist Tim Shipman in The Spectator writes , externalthat "it is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture."There is something in this. Take Rishi Sunak's Downing Street operation and Boris Johnson's. They were wildly different culturally, reflecting the very different characters at their helm. Would all the things that happened during Partygate under Johnson have happened under Sunak? Unlikely, I would have thought.Some within Reform, who are full of admiration for Nigel Farage's chutzpah and gift as a communicator, are desperate to see a behind-the-scenes cultural shift that minimises the chances of further embarrassments. And, alongside that, a step up in the infrastructure and personnel to match.Farage's team express frustration that this is precisely what they have been doing, but some are telling them internally they need to move more quickly.Both Orr and Jukes will be missed profoundly by those inside the party.Privately, some wonder if Orr may yet return.Jukes, who has been a pivotal and loyal figure in Team Farage for years, was already dividing his time between the UK and the United States as his wife and baby are on the other side of the Atlantic.Perhaps, some senior figures suggest, his immediate future might be in America. Does he return when the general election is nearer? Let's see.Reform leave Birmingham winded and wounded by the last few days, their days in the sun overshadowed.The question is how they deal with this and respond to it, in the coming weeks and months.

schema.headline: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach

title: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway
description: The Prince of Wales will attend the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday in Oslo, Buckingham Palace has announced.Also going to the funeral
body: The Prince of Wales will attend the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday in Oslo, Buckingham Palace has announced.Also going to the funeral, in a personal capacity, is Princess Anne, who is godmother to Norway's new monarch, King Haakon VIII.The late King Harald, a popular, modernising figure who had been on the Norwegian throne for 35 years, died last month at the age of 89.Royal sources say Prince William's attendance, representing his father King Charles, follows the convention that the monarch does not usually go to the funeral of another head of state.Large crowds are expected for the farewell to King Harald on 9 September, with a funeral procession to be followed by a service at Oslo Cathedral.Thousands have queued to pay their respects to the late king, during his lying in state in the chapel of the Royal Palace in the Norwegian capital.At the funeral, alongside Prince William, will be the widowed Queen Sonja, members of the Norwegian royal family including new King Haakon VIII, and other European royals.The service will be followed by a private burial in Norway's royal mausoleum in the Akershus Fortress.

schema.headline: Prince William to attend King Harald's funeral in Norway

title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
description: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what ap
body: Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board. In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening.""I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film."The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody."Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate. Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics. "They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said. He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy". Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations. He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days". They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats. They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029. They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest. Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage. But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.   What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake. One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions". No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty". And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage". Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said. But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say." But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing. Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

schema.headline: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks

title: Hull City on course to avoid relegation after seven points from three matches?
description: Figure caption, Aston Villa still winless after stalemate at HullByAdwaidh RajanBBC Sport journalist"Maybe expect to fight for a Champions League plac
body: Figure caption, Aston Villa still winless after stalemate at HullByAdwaidh RajanBBC Sport journalist"Maybe expect to fight for a Champions League place?"Sergej Jakirovic could not resist a joke when asked about Hull City's remarkable start to life back in the Premier League on BBC Match of the Day."No, of course it is early," the head coach was quick to follow up.Three games into a season is indeed too small a sample size to predict a club's fortunes. But with seven points from a possible nine, three clean sheets and only two points behind early pacesetters Manchester City, the Hull supporters can be forgiven for dreaming a little."It's huge for our confidence coming up into the Premier League," defender John Egan told Sky Sports."The start is important. We got the win the first day [against Manchester United] and I think that gave everyone confidence."If history is anything to go by, the Tigers may already have gone a long way towards securing their most important objective of the 2025-26 season - preserving their top-flight status.No newly promoted side has been relegated after taking seven or more points from their opening three Premier League games. Looking beyond promoted sides, only three teams have gone down after doing so.It might be far too early to settle any survival talks but, following another impressive outing in a 0-0 draw against Aston Villa on Saturday, there is no doubting Hull have given themselves the perfect platform to build on.From League One scare to Premier League heightsAs recently as last year Hull avoided relegation to League One only on goal difference. Fast-forward 16 months and they are now going toe to toe with the big names of the Premier League.The turnaround can be traced back to the arrival of Jakirovic before last season. The former Bosnia international joined a club under a transfer embargo, confining them to free transfers and loans, but still made them promotion contenders.Jakirovic guided Hull to a play-off win against a Millwall side who finished three places and 10 points above them, before Oli McBurnie's last-gasp winner against Middlesbrough secured top-flight football.And Hull did not stay still in the summer.They were the busiest Premier League side with 18 new signings for about £150m, with six of them, including £22m midfielder Tim Iroegbunam from Everton, arriving on deadline day."I know the core of my team. This is the Championship players," said Jakirovic, who signed a two-year contract extension on Friday."We brought the players in to put some quality there."The big problem for me is who didn't have a pre-season. This is a very big problem. But we will try."For example, on Tuesday [against Sunderland in the Carabao Cup], we will use that to give minutes, and at the end they will get a new chance."Figure caption, Hull 0-0 Aston Villa - Jakirovic reaction'Our goal is to collect 38-40 points' The result? Hull have beaten Michael Carrick's United and fellow promoted side Coventry City before holding Europa League winners Villa.Defensively, they have been outstanding.Only Charlton in 1998-99 and Huddersfield Town in 2017-18 had kept clean sheets in each of their first three league games after promotion to the Premier League."The work goes into it on the training pitch," said Egan, who is part of the three-man defence, alongside Semi Ajayi and Nobel Mendy, that has yet to be breached."It probably started in the play-offs when we moved to that shape. We have a lot of experience and it all helps."We've got a lot of lads who want to work together, defend for each other, and so far, so good. We just have to keep improving."Hull are also comfortable without possession.No team has had less of the ball this season than Hull (29%). Since 2003-04, only West Ham in 2023-24 (27%) have had a lower figure over their first three matches.Hull's rise is in stark contrast to last season's Championship winners Coventry, who are yet to open their account after three games.Only one of the previous 12 promoted sides have survived after doing so - Southampton in 2012-13.Yet Jakirovic knows Hull's work is far from done.Wolves in 2011-12, West Brom in 2017-18 and Leeds United in 2022-23 are the three teams who were relegated despite collecting seven points from their opening three matches.That equates to only 4% of the 78 teams to have collected seven points after three games and still go down.It might be a low probability, but Hull do not want to take any chances."This is a great result for us," Jakirovic said after his side threatened to claim all three points in the closing stages against Villa at MKM Stadium."Seven points. Three games. Clean sheet. Let's move on."Our goal is to collect the points. I think around 38-40 points, so as soon as possible to get these points."

schema.headline: Hull City on course to avoid relegation after seven points from three matches?

title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
description: The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate
body: The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University College London explained."He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities."Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.

schema.headline: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

title: Reform promises to increase tax-free personal allowance to £15,000
description: Reform UK is promising to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000, if it wins the next general election.Robert Jenrick, the party's econom
body: Reform UK is promising to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000, if it wins the next general election.Robert Jenrick, the party's economic spokesman, has pledged to introduce the tax cut within the first 100 days if he became chancellor saying it would provide "money that people really need right now".It is seen by Reform insiders as the flagship policy announcement of its conference and perhaps their biggest tax policy between now and the general election.Asked about two senior Reform aides being investigated by the party following a Channel 4 News undercover broadcast into claims about funding, Jenrick told the BBC Nigel Farage had acted swiftly and they had been suspended. In undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totalled £500,000.Electoral law sets out that to be a donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.Farage said on Friday that his party had "done nothing wrong" and had taken "no illegal money. In fact no money was taken at all."Jukes denied wrongdoing and said he was stepping away from politics "in order to clear my name". Orr told Sky News he would cooperate fully with the party's internal investigation.Orr is an associate professor of Philosophy of Religion at Cambridge University's Faculty of Divinity, and responding to the Channel 4 News and Verbatim report, Cambridge University said it was "looking into these matters".Jenrick told the Today programme that the party had taken legal advice and it did not believe it had done anything wrong.Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported the party to the Metropolitan Police.The Electoral Commission has said it is considering "all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit" and was in contact with the police.On tax measures, Reform estimates that increasing the tax-free threshold by £2,430 would save most taxpayers £500 a year and 2.9 million people would stop paying income tax altogether. It says the policy would cost £17.7bn in the first year, rising to £21bn by the fifth year and could be paid for through £80bn of public spending cuts the party plans to make. Jenrick told BBC Breakfast Reform would pay for the policy by "cutting out the waste".Reform has said its spending cuts would include a £50bn reduction in welfare spending.Half of the £353bn of welfare spending goes on the state pension, but Reform has said it will not cut this proportion.The bulk of the funding would come from reducing the cost of welfare, Jenrick said, by not paying benefits to people who are not British citizens and helping people who are off work due to their mental health back into jobs. Jenrick also said the UK would "stop paying foreign aid to rich countries", adding that "we should be looking after British people first"."Yes, we'll pay for disaster relief but the vast majority of that budget should be spent on the priorities of our own people," he said. Reform hopes to raise £10bn by scrapping net-zero programmes and Jenrick said, as the UK only amounted to 1% of the world's emissions, it was not sensible to be trying to decarbonise faster than other countries as that was "just impoverishing our own people".The party hopes to raise £8bn by reducing the number of civil servants and £7.1bn by capping the foreign aid budget.The policy was announced at Jenrick's speech on the last day of the party's conference in Birmingham."As chancellor, I will wake each morning with one purpose. To make Britain a better place to be a worker than it was the day before," he said."1.3 million were dragged into paying tax last year alone. Why? Because the tax-free allowance has been stuck at 12 and a half grand since 2021. And Labour has frozen it until 2031. "That betrayal costs a full-time worker on the minimum wage more than £750 a year. And now for the first time, the freeze means they're going to be taxing the state pension. What a disgrace."He said that if he failed to deliver the tax cut in his first Budget he would resign as chancellor."No ifs, no buts, I'll be gone."In its manifesto before the general election in 2024, Reform said it wanted to lift the threshold to £20,000. Jenrick told conference activists this remains his long-term aim.The personal allowance threshold currently stands at £12,570. Anyone earning more than £100,000 starts to lose their personal allowance. For every £2 earned above the threshold the basic allowance decreases by £1.Shortly after becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham told the Times that the "frustration" of people in his Makerfield constituency about the frozen allowance had "lodged in my mind".He later said that "all of this would be looked at" in the upcoming Budget but that any change would be "difficult given the financial circumstances".

schema.headline: Reform promises to increase tax-free personal allowance to £15,000

title: Jaguar Land Rover confirms plans for voluntary job cuts
description: Car manufacturer Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought pro
body: Car manufacturer Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.The firm said it needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years as it seeks to adapt to "evolving global market conditions".It was reported by The Times on Saturday that as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.The firm told the BBC it had not confirmed the numbers. It said the decision to cut jobs was to help "simplify" the organisation as well as "improve efficiency and build greater resilience"."Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said."We will share further information with our colleagues first."Unite general secretary. Sharon Graham. said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time."Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses adding that she and Business Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would be meeting JLR's chief executive, PB Balaji, next week."This is an incredibly worrying and stressful time for JLR workers," said Unite national officer, Des Quinn. "Unite is working round the clock to deliver the best possible outcome."Meanwhile a government spokesperson said significant action had been taken to support the UK automotive industry by lowering electricity bills for manufacturers as well as financial support for the manufacture and sale of zero emission vehicles.Reynolds was also understood to have spoken with West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, about supporting the business and its staff.JLR said over the past three years, it had strengthened its brands and had prepared for production of its next generation of vehicles.In July, the company said it expected fewer than 300 people would leave the firm under cost savings plans announced at the time.The company has its global headquarters at Whitley, Coventry, and manufacturing sites in Solihull and Wolverhampton as well as Halewood on Merseyside.It employs about 30,000 people in its UK operations, with approximately 10,000 people employed at plants overseas.The cyber attack in September 2025 led to the shut down of all manufacturing at JLR for several weeks, meaning not a single vehicle rolled off its production lines.That led to a 27% drop in overall production at the company, which is one of the West Midlands' biggest employers.The overall cost of the cyber-attack and the subsequent loss of manufacturing was estimated to be £1.9bn.In June, the firm announced it planned to cut about £1.7bn in costs over the coming years to help towards its recovery from the attack.JLR had indicated at the time that it would make the savings through cuts in areas such as materials, warranty and fixed costs.

schema.headline: Jaguar Land Rover confirms plans for voluntary job cuts

title: Sibling rivalry: When parents play financial favourites
description: 'My parents won't lend me £10k but helped my brother': When families play financial favouritesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, One US study su
body: 'My parents won't lend me £10k but helped my brother': When families play financial favouritesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, One US study suggests around 15% of siblings have had conflicts over moneyByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsDo your parents have a favourite child and give them more money, gifts or help?Financial favouritism can cause jealousy and resentment long into adulthood and, in some cases, even spark legal disputes after a parent dies. But experts say there are strategies that can help you avoid it.John says his parents, who have always supported his younger brother, recently refused to lend him £10,000 towards a house deposit after he broke up with his partner.This was despite the money being "well within their financial grasp", he says.His parents had previously given his brother a deposit to buy a home and subsidised his living expenses.John, 47, whose real name we have changed, says he was viewed as the more academic one growing up and expected to stand on his "own two feet" financially, while his brother, 42, struggled to make his way in the world and was "coddled".He says the favouritism has made him believe "the needs of others take precedence over my own", leaving him feeling "isolated" and affecting friendships and romantic relationships.'Powerful emotional meaning'Forums like Mumsnet and Reddit, external are full of posts complaining about siblings being shown preferential treatment regarding money. Common gripes include the amount of financial support adult children have received, external from their parents during their lifetime, the way inheritance is divided, external, and whether a sibling has supported their parents more than others, external.Dr Fenia Christodoulidi, from counselling service Relate, says that disagreements about money between siblings are rarely just about the money itself.  "Financial support from parents often carries a powerful emotional meaning and some siblings tend to interpret differences in support as signs of favouritism, unequal love or a lack of recognition." She adds that even when parents have "practical reasons" for treating their children differently, failing to communicate these clearly can "leave room for misunderstanding and resentment".Those reasons might include an adult child needing more support because they earn significantly less, have an illness, or have to pay more to get on the housing ladder due to rising prices, external.'It's never been a problem'Image caption, Ellis, 26, says there is no financial favourite in her familyEllis, who works in finance in London, tells the BBC that she and her siblings have had "different levels of support at different times" from their parents and it's never been a problem.Image caption, Tasha says her siblings have had disagreementsBut her colleague Tasha, the youngest of seven, says her siblings have fallen out over perceived favouritism, even though she thinks her parents treat them all the same."I just think people sometimes get a bit uncertain or jealous and that's quite normal," says the 33-year-old. "Sometimes people stop talking for a bit or go to process what they are feeling, and they come back together and they just hash it out."'Open conversations help'Having "open conversations about expectations and the reasons behind decisions" can help reduce feelings of resentment about money, Christodoulidi says.But for some, it's not that easy. "Talking about money is verboten in my family - be it salaries or savings or financial assistance," says John. "Any time I've tried to air my feelings my parents just become evasive so now I don't bother."John says he is now planning his financial future on the basis he won't have any inheritance - although he expects to be asked to step in if his parents get ill or lose capacity.He says he has a "great relationship with his brother" but feels resentment towards his parents for creating the "imbalance" between them.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Open conversations can help reduce feelings of resentmentClaire Webb, a solicitor and mediator at Family Solutions Now, regularly helps siblings who have disputes over inheritance and other money matters."One sibling might argue the other was given more money earlier on in life, say, to buy a house, and that the parents said this would be reflected in the will. "Then the will says, 'everything should be shared equally'. So you have all of that historic feeling of unfairness being dredged up."To avoid conflict, she says parents need to be clear with their children about what they want while they are still alive. 'A deep-down family bond'Siblings who do fall out should consider mediation before taking legal action, she adds. This is when a trained professional helps them remedy their problems.The good news is, siblings who take the legal route more often than not reach an amicable solution. "Most of the time there is a deep-down family bond - and if you can crack what started the problem they often find a way through."Tips for resolving money quarrels between siblings1. Recognise what's behind the row: It may be about feeling valued or treated fairly, rather than the money itself2. Avoid making assumptions about a sibling's financial situation or the reasons behind parental decisions3. Encourage open, respectful conversations where everyone has the opportunity to explain how they feel4. Parents should communicate their intentions as clearly as possible, particularly if they are supporting children differently for practical reasons5. Consider family counselling if conversations repeatedly become stuck or emotionally charged6. Consider mediation before taking legal action in inheritance disputes.  7. Choose powers of attorney carefully: Parents usually appoint their children to oversee their care and finances if they get ill or lose mental capacity. But if there's a risk they'll fall out, they can appoint someone else including a solicitor. Sources: Relate, Family Now Solutions

schema.headline: Sibling rivalry: When parents play financial favourites

title: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'
description: For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.Jeremy Clarkson
body: For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May built one of television's most recognisable partnerships, meaning anyone taking over The Grand Tour was always going to face a daunting task.Now YouTubers James Engelsman and Thomas Holland and, perhaps most unexpectedly, train enthusiast-turned-internet star Francis Bourgeois are stepping into their shoes for the new series.And, with initial reviews generally mixed, they knew they had some convincing to do."They literally changed the car world," Holland says of the previous trio.He understands why some fans have questions about whether the show should continue with anyone else."They're completely justified to feel that, because they did the same thing that we did - which is grow up watching Clarkson, Hammond and May."The show was a very important part of our lives as car enthusiasts."Engelsman says they themselves initially had many of the same doubts that viewers will have."We've had all the same reactions that the audience has had to every part of this process like, 'Who would do that? What an idiot.'"We've been through it all and we're just lucky enough to have come out the other side and realised, 'OK, this is actually all stuff that could work.'""Now we've filmed it, I'm just excited to show the world," Bourgeois says. "We've done our absolute best and the critics will be critics and I hope that we will prove them wrong."Holland adds that he hopes people will give the show a chance before judging."Have a watch and if you don't like it, you're well within your rights, I can't force anyone to like anything."For a show built around the chemistry of its three former presenters, finding a replacement trio with such chemistry was always going to be as important as finding people who knew about cars.Engelsman and Holland are an already established double act as the presenters of Throttle House, a motoring YouTube channel with more than three million subscribers.The bigger unknown was who would become their third presenter.That search eventually led the show's producers to Francis Bourgeois, a social media star better known for standing on railway platforms than behind the wheel of a supercar.Engelsman says he and Holland had done chemistry testing with a number of people, but Bourgeois immediately felt different."As soon as Francis showed up, we were like: 'That guy'," Holland says.Bourgeois remembers their first meeting taking place on a leather sofa in a hotel outside Basingstoke, where they mostly talked about what cars they owned.By the time filming began, Holland says there was no need to consciously work out how to make the three-person dynamic function as "it just worked and clicked immediately".While the chemistry came quickly, actually finding out they had the job was much less straightforward. Engelsman says there was "no immediate moment" when they were formally told they had been chosen."It was the most gradual thing," he says.He and Holland initially thought they were simply part of a wider audition process, but then found themselves repeatedly being invited into writers' rooms and asked for their views on ideas for the show.For Bourgeois, that uncertainty may have been helpful as he admits he'd "just fall apart and start crying" if he'd found out about the job.There is a clear generational shift with the new presenters, all three of whom built their profiles on social media - and critics have been mixed on how successfully that translates to The Grand Tour. The Independent's three-star review, external described the reboot as "all rather safe" and said the presenters feel "stilted".The Guardian's review, external agreed and called the trio a "decent, if slightly anonymous, presence" who seem "quite meek and pleasant, and without any obvious dynamic".But it did praise Bourgeois, with Stuart Heritage calling him "the most enthusiastic enthusiast currently working on planet Earth".The FT also awarded the show three-stars, external and said that while the big budget spectacles are enjoyable to watch, they also feel "a little muted".It added that "the real question is whether a series that has been driven by big personalities like Clarkson, May and Hammond can survive with a new team".Hammond tells BBC News he tuned in for The Grand Tour's return and said it was great to see the new team getting going."That's the most important thing for them is to make their show. We made our show and we're really good at being us. They're going to be really good at being them," he says.Hammond says the audience need to "give them the chance" to show that.

schema.headline: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'

title: Thieves steal 70,000 pints of Guinness in two lorries
description: Thieves have stolen more than 800 barrels of Guinness by driving off from a depot with two HGV trailers. About 70,000 pints worth of the stout, estima
body: Thieves have stolen more than 800 barrels of Guinness by driving off from a depot with two HGV trailers. About 70,000 pints worth of the stout, estimated to be worth £115,000, were taken from Whitehouse Industrial Estate on Aston Lane in Runcorn on Monday, Cheshire Police said.One wagon-load was taken at about 19:45 BST and a second one was stolen at about 21:30.  The stolen barrels - which each would hold about 88 pints - had been destined for pubs, the force added. Det Sgt McClatchy said: "It is famously said that 'Guinness is good for you', but that is only the case when it has been bought and paid for."

title: Police probe after child dies in woodland in Cheslyn Hay
description: A police investigation has been launched following the unexplained death of a child in woodland. Emergency services were called to reports of a child
body: A police investigation has been launched following the unexplained death of a child in woodland. Emergency services were called to reports of a child in cardiac arrest on land near Strawberry Lane, Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at about 08:45 BST on Saturday.An air ambulance was sent to the scene, but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.The force, which has not confirmed the age of the child or any other details, is currently treating the death as unexplained.Roads in the area were closed throughout the day while investigations took place and officers were expected to remain at the scene throughout the evening.

title: Dame Prue Leith: 'When you're old, you don't give a toss'
description: Prue Leith: 'You come into your own growing old'Image caption, Dame Prue Leith says growing old is "unstressful" as she prepares to discuss ageing at
body: Prue Leith: 'You come into your own growing old'Image caption, Dame Prue Leith says growing old is "unstressful" as she prepares to discuss ageing at the Cheltenham Literature FestivalByMaisie LillywhiteGloucestershire and Jon SmithBBC Radio Gloucestershire"When you're old, you don't give a toss what anyone thinks, really, so you feel very free. You can have a snooze in the afternoon, and nobody thinks that's odd."Dame Prue Leith is celebrating her perceived joys of the golden years as she prepares to discuss "Growing Old Disgracefully" with fellow authors Gyles Brandreth and Kathy Lette.The trio will take to the stage at this year's Cheltenham Literature Festival on 15 October to prove to the audience ageing is "not the dreaded thing" it is made out to be, the former Bake Off judge said.Dame Prue said: "You come into your own, you don't care what people think, you're not going to change. And so the world has to just put up with it."At 86, the restaurateur and cookery writer has reflected on her younger years and has decided that growing old is good fun, although she acknowledged it may be different for those who are "old and lonely and ill"."When I think of my teenage years, I think they were really stressful," Dame Prue said. "I was always bringing the wrong boys home, and I was quarrelling with my parents, and I didn't know what I wanted to do."I was sort of lost and didn't believe in myself at all... I wanted a boyfriend, couldn't get one, you know. Old age is unstressful."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Dame Prue said she is "very happy" living in the CotswoldsThe talk at The Times and Sunday Times Forum in Montpellier Terrace next month will not be Dame Prue's first time at the festival, which launched in the spa town in 1949.She last appeared at the event in 2018, but outside of her career, she is no stranger to the area."I love Cheltenham; I often go even if I'm not doing anything, but it's a great festival," she said.'I'm very happy here'On screen, Dame Prue showcases her nearby home in Prue Leith's Cotswolds Kitchen, which, she said, gives her an outlet to be "a bossy woman"."I've persuaded my husband to come into it, and he's very funny," she said."It's quite domestic, and it's filmed in our house, so that's even better. It's a great house, and I'm very happy here; I'm in the middle of the Cotswolds. "We built this house four or five years ago, and it's got a great garden... I'm looking out the window as I speak and it's just rolling Cotswolds, fields, can't see a single building."Growing Old Disgracefully will be held at The Times and Sunday Times Forum on 15 October at 13:00.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Gloucestershire

title: Major disruption as grass fire hits Heathrow train links
description: Trains to and from Heathrow Airport have been halted after a trackside grass fire caused delays and cancellations. National Rail said "major disruptio
body: Trains to and from Heathrow Airport have been halted after a trackside grass fire caused delays and cancellations. National Rail said "major disruption" was expected until the end of Saturday following the incident which began shortly after 16:00 BST.A statement said all lines were blocked between London Paddington station and Heathrow's terminals, as well as Reading, due to "a failure of the electricity supply caused by a fire next to the track".An update from Network Rail Western late on Saturday said the fire had been extinguished, but warned that disruption would continue, possibly into Sunday morning for some services.It comes hours after a separate grass fire on Heathrow's airfield shut a runway earlier on Saturday.Pictures on social media showed crowds of stranded passengers at Paddington, one of London's main rail hubs.London Fire Brigade said six fire engines and around 40 crew members were tackling the blaze near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington.Great Western Railway, external cancelled its services to Reading and no Elizabeth line or Heathrow Express services were running between Paddington and Heathrow on Saturday night.The airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys, adding that the Piccadilly line, which runs services to the airport, also has delays.Network Rail Western said some services on Sunday morning could face delays and cancellations, caused by trains being displaced by the disruption. Earlier on Saturday, Heathrow's southern runway was closed while crews tackled a grass fire on the airfield. It caused some disruption with at least two flights diverted elsewhere. Heathrow apologised for any disruption and said the fire was extinguished quickly. That comes weeks after another grass fire near Heathrow's southern runway which forced 18 flights to divert and destroyed a large area of grassland. While weather has cooled across much of the UK in recent days following record-breaking heat over the summer, fire crews have still been warning of wildfire risks.The Met Office's Fire Severity Index, external shows that if a wildfire was to occur, it would have a "high" fire severity in most of south-east England and some of the Midlands.The fire severity is "exceptional", the highest level on the index, in some parts of London including Heathrow, as well as on the Essex and Suffolk coasts.

title: Russia-Ukraine war: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks
description: US President Donald Trump's top negotiators have met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as efforts to end the war in Ukraine gather pace.Foot
body: US President Donald Trump's top negotiators have met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as efforts to end the war in Ukraine gather pace.Footage released by the Kremlin showed Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner being greeted by Putin, who said the current situation "is not so easy". He added Russia would explain "how we see the situation".Witkoff thanked Putin for agreeing with Ukraine to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days. On Sunday the envoys will travel to Kyiv for more talks.On Friday, Trump said Witkoff and Kushner were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war". So far, efforts by the US and its allies to broker a peace deal have failed.At Saturday's talks in the Kremlin, Putin also said that "in any case, whatever happens, such contacts are undoubtedly always useful". He also thanked Trump for his peacemaking efforts.He told the envoys that he was "comfortable" working with them, adding: "Of course on our side there is quite a high level of trust during this work."The talks – which continued behind closed doors in Putin's official residence in the heart of the Russian capital – lasted for three hours, according to Russian state media.Zelensky said earlier on Saturday that he had spoken to the envoys, who have "already begun working with the Russian side today". "The plan for tomorrow's diplomatic engagements in Kyiv, involving the US team, has been approved. We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation," he added."From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv."Russian state media reported that President Vladimir Putin had ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv for three days due to the US visit.In televised remarks, Putin said Russia had not agreed to a ceasefire for the rest of Ukraine outside of the capital. The Russian president said he would "ensure the security of the negotiating process" and of the mediators.Kushner and Witkoff have visited Russia several times but the talks on Sunday would be the first in Ukraine. It is not clear how the US envoys will be travelling from Moscow to Kyiv.Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.Delegations from Ukraine have attended talks in the US over the past 18 months.Earlier on Saturday, Zelensky said Russia had fired "demonstrative" strikes on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of his planned meeting with the US.Ukraine's president added: "Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport."Zelensky said on Friday he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to do the same for Ukraine.He also said an overnight Russian strike on a civilian building in the Dnipro region killed four people and injured five others.Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow comes just over a week after a rare visit to the Russian capital by the head of the CIA, John Ratcliffe. There was no official comment from Washington or the Kremlin on what was discussed. Speaking last week, Trump described the meeting as "semi-routine".Last year, the US, Ukraine and Russia separately suggested that a deal to end the war was edging closer following a flurry of talks brokered by the Americans. European allies also held talks in Paris but discussions ultimately ended without a breakthrough. Key disagreements remain between the warring sides on issues such as territory and security guarantees for Ukraine. In recent months, both Russia and Ukraine have intensified their aerial attacks as fighting continues.Ukraine said it has struggled to repel ballistic missile attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets.

schema.headline: Russia-Ukraine war: US envoys meet Putin in Moscow for Ukraine talks
